subject: Aligning on TTFT targets and streaming mode for FastMetrics pilot
messages:
From: Alice Nguyen <alice@fastmetrics.com>
To: Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 24 May 2027 13:05:00 -07:00
Subject: Quick follow-up after demo — TTFT priorities

Thanks for the demo today — Samir and I appreciated the walkthrough. Two quick recap items from our side so we can lock the pilot scope: 

1) Primary metric: time-to-first-token (TTFT) from request arrival to first token delivered. Target is 120ms p95 for the most common path. This matters because our UI shows the first token to the user and we need that to feel instantaneous.

2) Streaming preference: we currently use SSE in prod for other subsystems, but we're open to WebSockets if there are performance benefits. Main ask is consistent chunk cadence (no bursts that create perceived stuttering).

Can you confirm Redwood's recommended approach (SSE vs WS) for our traffic profile and what concurrency/throughput we should size for? Also please share any pilot test harness we can run against.

Attachments: demo-recording.mp4 (mp4)

Thanks,
Alice Nguyen
VP Product, FastMetrics
From: Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>
To: Alice Nguyen <alice@fastmetrics.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 25 May 2027 09:15:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick follow-up after demo — TTFT priorities

Hi Alice — great talking yesterday. Short answers up front, followed by proposed next steps.

Summary answers:
- TTFT: 120ms p95 is aggressive but achievable on Redwood hosted inference with a few caveats (model size, prompt priming, network egress). We recommend an initial pilot target of 150ms p95 to avoid early false negatives, then iterate to 120ms once we validate prefix caching.
- Streaming: SSE is simpler for your stack and has lower handshake overhead, but WebSocket gives slightly better per-connection latency variability under high concurrency. Either is fine; choice depends on client constraints.
- Chunk cadence: aim for 1–2 short chunks (~20–40ms apart) for the first 200–300 tokens, then aggregate to ~200ms cadence thereafter to reduce tail noise.

Next steps I propose:
1) Ben to propose an initial SLO matrix and an emulation harness you can run.
2) We'll run a 48-hour pilot with a synthetic traffic pattern that mirrors your web UI (50 concurrent users, median session length 18s).
3) Share a small sample of typical prompts and expected max context (so we can choose quantization and kernel path).

I've attached a starter TTFT matrix we use for pilots.

Attachments: redwood-ttft-matrix.xlsx (xlsx)

Best,
Connor O'Brien
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
To: Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Cc: Alice Nguyen <alice@fastmetrics.com>, Samir Rao <samir@fastmetrics.com>
Date: Mon, 25 May 2027 11:00:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Quick follow-up after demo — TTFT priorities

Adding technical detail from infra/R&D to make the pilot concrete. Key recommendations and tradeoffs: 

1) Baseline targets (pilot):
   - TTFT: start at 150ms p95; expected median ~60–90ms on hosted L4 instances with prefix caching enabled.
   - Throughput: target 1,200 rps sustained for the pilot traffic pattern (50 concurrent users with bursts).
   - Concurrency: test window should include bursts to 400 concurrent in a worst-case ramp-up profile to validate autoscaling.

2) Streaming mode guidance:
   - SSE: pros = simple, works through proxies, low handshake. Cons = each connection is unidirectional and some older proxies buffer events (rare).
   - WebSocket: pros = bi-directional, smaller per-frame overhead at scale. Cons = slightly more complex auth renewal, requires sticky routing in some infra.
   - Recommendation: pilot with SSE (matches your stack); run a WebSocket comparison run during the pilot for 24–48 hours to measure p95 delta.

3) Chunk cadence and tokenization:
   - Initial emit: send a small priming chunk (~6–10 tokens) within first 40–80ms to achieve perceived responsiveness.
   - Follow-up chunks: 20–50ms cadence for first N tokens (N based on median response length you share), then fold into 150–250ms windows to amortize kernel overhead.

4) Telemetry & success criteria:
   - Measure TTFT p50/p95/p99 and UI-perceived jitter (stddev of inter-chunk intervals).
   - Define pass criteria: p95 <= 150ms and perceived jitter <= 40ms for 90% of sessions.

5) Test harness deliverables:
   - We will provide a k6 script and a lightweight client that can run SSE and WS patterns against a Redwood pilot endpoint.

I'll prepare the k6 artifacts and a sample traffic manifest once Connor confirms sample prompts and context sizes.

-Ben
Ben Carter
Principal SRE, Redwood Inference
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

- Ben: produce k6 script + SSE/WS client and upload to the Drive link; include run instructions and expected dashboard queries. Target delivery: 2027-05-28 12:00 PDT.
- Marissa: coordinate pilot window with FastMetrics and draft a short mutual action plan (MAP) including success criteria and timeline.
- Ops note: ensure we enable prefix caching and a temporary 2x autoscale cap for the pilot to avoid cold-start tail.

I'll loop in Solutions if we need a customer-facing runbook. Connor — can you confirm when Alice can take the k6 run? Also please add the HubSpot link to the MAP once the deal is created.
